source.title: A Counterexample to Fourier Alignment in Single-Neuron Modular Addition

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses grokking as context, but its results concern single-neuron Fourier alignment and dead-neuron dynamics, not delayed train/test generalization or any of the listed grokking versions.
record.gate_note: The paper does not report training or test accuracy trajectories, a grokking delay, dataset-size effects, or progress measures anticipating a generalization jump. Its results concern Fourier-energy alignment in one-neuron modular-addition training; the rows below record those adjacent findings as versions none. Its citations to grokking work are background, not results from those studies.
record.test_reason: This is a purely theoretical paper about whether a single ReLU neuron trained on modular addition must align to one Fourier frequency. Its own results are counterexamples: dead-neuron and persistent one-example trajectories whose Fourier energy is 2/(p−1) per nonzero class. It reports no train or test accuracy, no generalization delay, no dataset-size effect and no progress measures. Remark 1.4 states that a single neuron cannot solve the modular-addition table, so there is no generalizing algorithm to compare across runs (V6). Grokking appears only as motivation, through citations of Nanda et al. and a remark that the persistent branch resembles memorization.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors conclude that single-frequency (monosemantic) Fourier alignment is not forced by training a single neuron on modular addition, while Fourier structure itself is not absent. They show this via dead-neuron and persistent one-example memorization counterexamples. They note the question stays open for everywhere-positive activations such as softplus, and they make no grokking accuracy claims.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies one ReLU neuron trained by exact full-table cross-entropy on modular addition, chiefly through theoretical continuous-time trajectories and additional smooth-activation and fixed-step gradient-descent constructions; it does not reproduce the grokking training recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports distinct outcomes under selected Clarke trajectories, all Clarke trajectories, the ReLU′(0)=0 convention, smooth dead-zone activations, and fixed-step vanilla full-batch gradient descent. It explicitly limits the smooth-activation result to activations with an exact dead half-line and the discrete result to vanilla fixed-step full-batch gradient descent.

fits_no_version.finding: Single-neuron full-table cross-entropy training on modular addition can end in dead or persistent states whose Fourier energy is spread equally across all nonzero classes, on open sets of initializations and under several dynamics.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Single-frequency Fourier alignment is not forced by single-neuron modular-addition training.

fits_no_version.finding: On the persistent sliding trajectory one table entry is fit, every other entry keeps loss log p, and the parameter norm diverges.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A single neuron can persistently memorize one example instead of learning the table.

record.problems: The evidence is theoretical and concerns one-neuron Fourier alignment, not grokking train/test accuracy. The paper reports no empirical accuracy curves or dataset-size sweep. Its principal dead-neuron construction initially uses a selected Clarke trajectory, although the appendix supplies stronger results for every Clarke trajectory and other stated dynamics.

untested.parts: All of it: no accuracy trajectories, no delayed test-accuracy rise, no training-set-size comparison.
All of it: no time course of a generalizing circuit and no progress measure predicting a generalization jump. Fourier structure is analysed only at the limit, for a model that cannot generalize.
All of it: no non-algorithmic data and no initialization-scale or weight-norm sweep tied to delayed generalization.
All of it: no LLM training.
All of it: the setting explicitly has no weight decay, and there is no critical dataset size or ungrokking test.
All of it: initialization-dependent Fourier outcomes are shown for one neuron that cannot solve the task, not for algorithms learned by networks that solve it.
All of it: the ReLU′(0) convention and the fixed-step gradient-descent constructions concern Fourier alignment, not grokking delays.

record.verdict_notes: The rows are correctly linked to none of the versions. The evidence is theorems, not experiments. The paper is not an original source for any version. The appendix was drafted with an AI system and then reviewed by the author.

versions.untested_parts: No training/test accuracy trajectory, chance-level test performance, delayed test-accuracy rise, or training-set-size comparison.
No time-course measurement of a generalizing circuit or memorizing components, and no progress measure predicting a test-accuracy jump.
No non-algorithmic data or initialization-scale/weight-norm sweep testing grokking-like delays.
No weight-decay or low-norm efficiency account, critical dataset size, or ungrokking test.
No comparison of identifiable algorithms learned across runs, architectures, or hyperparameters.
No test of optimizer instability or floating-point softmax artifacts as causes of grokking delays.
